It went from being actual news about important things, to being click bait and YouTube videos or Facebook posts turned into an article.

From my perspective, it already started weak and transitioned into full on yellow journalism (with few exceptions). As far as I'm concerned, the "easily accessible" news outlets stand as completely untrustable. They may serve as sources that hint at information, at best.

It used to be newspapers, magazine, and television. Then the Internet came around. Suddenly there were a ton more options. However, that seems to have diluted the quality. Everyone with a keyboard and an agenda could call themselves a "journalist".

Worse was the traditional outlets response to the new competition. It seems as though every media outlet has gone the way of the lowest common denominator. Sensationalized tabloid reporting, click bait, and fear mongering all appear to be more common than they were 25 years ago.

Or maybe I'm just getting old and crotchety. Damned kids these days with their rock music.

One of the funny little changes I got to see was that, after 9/11 tv news decided there was too much information to just have one subject on the screen at a time, and started using tickers at the bottom of the screen... Those were nonexistent before 9/11. It's weird to think that some people have grown up with those always being there.

edit: the grammar were wrong

The news, once upon a time, reported to me.

Now the news tells me what/how to think about what it reports to me.

Compulsory Orwell reference.

If I need to shout something in order to be heard, I should contact a good journalist or reporter. Hey, thank you for your what you do. I hope you can always use your voices for good. My best wishes go out to you. My local newspapers have pretty great listeners.

News gathering used to be a process. There would be reporters who aggressively covered beats and worked sources. Now, newspapers and newsmagazines have slashed staff. These media outlets don't have the resources to truly cover news. There is are very, very few true investigative journalists. Instead, it's press release information distribution. I would venture to guess that 95 percent of the "news" in newspapers is something that someone WANTED published. True journalism is publishing the articles the powers that be do not want published.

And, there's no incentive for any media to spend the resources to have an investigative presence. One example: The Penn State sex scandal. A small Harrisburg newspaper broke the story, asked the tough questions, took all the time to gather the information. Do you think their circulation dramatically improved? Or advertisers flocked to them? No. And their web site didn't get anywhere close to the amount of clicks that sites such as Huffington Post did by covering the story by re-wording the Harrisburg paper's reporting.

Perhaps the non-profit investigative journalism model may work. But such organizations will be beholden to their funding sources.

Bottom line: Can't trust any media. Have to do your own research.

It used to be you picked up a newspaper and assumed the story you were reading was factual. Probably in most cases it was. It contained eye witness accounts of something that happened, it contained facts the reporter scraped together, and gave you a general overview of the incident - whatever that might have been.

Now, everything is re-reported. Someone writes a story and everyone else picks up on it - regurgitating it and adding little tidbits they plucked from other people regurgitating the story. The desire to fact check is overlooked by the desire to get the story out so others can regurgitate their added tidbits.

I don't trust the "news" today.
